extracted.intended_audience: readers researching Roger Ebert and standards for film criticism/journalism
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted evaluative principles and standards for journalism and film criticism as reflected in Roger Ebert's quoted views and reactions (e.g., purpose of criticism, tone of negative reviews, interpreting irony).

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenge narrow thinking / oppose political correctness that silences
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the purposes of journalism is to challenge that kind of thinking. And certainly one of the purposes of criticism is to break boundaries. It's also one of the purposes of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ebert criticized 'political correctness' as a rigid impulse to keep ideas within very narrow boundaries for fear of offending. As a normative standard, journalism/criticism/art should push against such constraints rather than conform to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize irony and humor; interpret authorial intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Ebert lamented that Adventures of Huckleberry Finn 'has regrettably been under fire in recent years from myopic advocates of Political Correctness, who do not have a bone of irony (or humor) in their bodies, and cannot tell the difference between what is said or done in the novel, and what Twain means by it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should distinguish between an author's use of irony/satire and literal endorsement; avoid literalist or myopic readings that conflate characters' actions/statements with authorial approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative reviews should entertain without insulting
rubrics_metrics.description: His negative reviews were invariably his most entertaining, and yet, he never insulted those who found something to admire in lesser films.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing harsh or negative criticism, aim for entertaining prose and wit but avoid ad hominem or demeaning attacks on audiences or those who appreciate the work; the goal is to enlighten, not merely to demean.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to enlighten and challenge readers; foster appetite for stronger work
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead, he hoped to enlighten readers, challenging them to think, while whetting their appetite for stronger work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviews should serve an educative function: provoke thought, guide taste toward higher-quality works, and help readers deepen appreciation rather than simply issuing verdicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Go beyond simple thumbs up/thumbs down; write with passion and film knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews went far deeper than simply thumbs up or thumbs down. He wrote with passion through a real knowledge of film and film history, and in doing so, helped many movies find their audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantive criticism should demonstrate historical/contextual knowledge and passionate engagement; avoid reducing evaluation to a binary label without explanation or context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reviews as a vehicle for broader ideas (Trojan horse for philosophy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Film reviews, as he wrote them, served as a Trojan horse for the delivery of bigger philosophical ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism can and sometimes should carry larger intellectual or philosophical commentary — reviews can introduce readers to wider cultural, ethical, or aesthetic questions via the lens of a film.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not require characters to represent their entire group
rubrics_metrics.description: Responding to criticism that a film was 'empty and amoral for Asian Americans,' Ebert argued: 'Asian-American characters have the right to be whoever the hell they want to be. They do not have to represent "their people"!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating representation, avoid demanding that individual characters bear the burden of representing an entire demographic; allow characters complexity and autonomy instead of treating them as proxies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critics and citizens should exercise freedom of speech; speak out responsibly
rubrics_metrics.description: He lamented that 'Most Americans don't understand the First Amendment, don't understand the idea of freedom of speech, and don't understand that it's the responsibility of the citizen to speak out.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit standard for critics: take civic responsibility seriously and use the platform to speak out; criticism is part of public discourse and carries an obligation to contribute thoughtful, informed arguments.
